The epitope-specific mAb AM14 neutralized infection of HEp-2 cells by all RSV strains tested, including strains A Long, A2, subtype B strain 18537, subtype B strain 9320, and subtypes A and B clinical strains. AM14 did not inhibit attachment of RSV to the surface of HEp-2 cells, suggesting that it prevents entry by blocking a step downstream of attachment. Monoclonal antibody-resistant mutants (MARMs) selected in HEp-2 cells produced four unique AM14-escape viruses, three with a single mutation in RSV F (L160S, N183K, or N426D), and a fourth virus containing three mutations in RSV F (I79M/R429S/H515N), confirming the importance of the epitope residues.

The epitope-specific motavizumab antibody neutralized RSV more potently than palivizumab, as determined in a flow cytometric assay.

The epitope-specific Motavizumab and the parent antibody Palivizumab neutralized RSV, as measured by a flow cytometry neutralization assay using HEp-2 cells infected with RSV-GFP. The mAb strongly inhibited fusion when added after attachment. The mAb, however, did not block cell surface attachment.

The epitope-specific D25 Fab or IgG neutralized RSV, as measured by a flow cytometry neutralization assay using HEp-2 cells infected with RSV-GFP. Human mAb AM22 (Fab or IgG) and mouse mAb 5C4, which recognize the same or a highly related epitope, also blocked RSV infection. The three mAbs strongly inhibited fusion when added after attachment. The mAbs, however, did not block cell surface attachment.
